body:
Handoff before the operator leaves: PR #1983, a stale-binary incident that affects TASK-1279, and I am winding the fanout down for the night

THREE THINGS, the middle one matters most.

1. PR #1983, TASK-1292, open and yours. +253, branch task-1292 (spec-named, as you asked). Same handover as before: I wrote the prompt, so no verdict from me.

The root cause is deeper than the spec described and I verified the central claim in the diff. The guard was not merely spec-keyed by choice — `member.pr` was only ever written at TERMINAL outcome via set_member_outcome, never while a member was mid-phase. So the PR-keyed scan had no live data to key on for a running reviewer, and the fallback matched only when the hold marker's reason text happened to name a spec still in the drive's in-phase set. The fix binds member.pr the moment a phase starts. That is why a sibling-spec reviewer was invisible rather than merely mis-matched, and it means the PR-keyed scan was dead code in the case it existed for.

Reported, not re-run by me: 5088 tests pass, fmt clean, head matches local.

2. A STALE BINARY DROVE PART OF TONIGHT, and TASK-1279 is the spec affected.

At about 17:35 `target/release/aida` was absent mid-`make build-fast`. The drain spawned its phase-1 child through PATH, which fell through to /home/joe/.local/bin/aida — the released 0.15.0 built 2026-09-11. Eight days and roughly thirty merges stale: no BUG-1265 hold-gate refinement, no BUG-1191 informational filter, no TASK-1291 full sweep, no BUG-1268 stale-base recovery.

Nothing reported it. drain status read active and the wave looked healthy. I found it only because `aida mailbox send --body-file` stopped existing mid-session — a flag I had been using for hours. The broken command was the symptom.

TASK-1279's run is the one driven by that binary. The blast radius is orchestration rather than authorship — codex reads the repo, so the code it writes is current — but the lease handling, phase logic, CI gating and PR shipping around it were all eight days old. Treat anything TASK-1279 produced tonight with more suspicion than usual, and if its PR looks odd that is the first hypothesis rather than the last.

This is TASK-1289's motivating scenario, happening to the orchestrator instead of to a guard. Worth noting on that spec: the preflight guards exist to stop a stale binary producing phantom drift, and the orchestrator that runs them has the same exposure with no equivalent protection.

I hardened my launcher rather than filing it — it now resolves the dev build by absolute path, refuses to launch while the binary is missing instead of falling through to PATH, re-checks after building since a failed build leaves nothing, and logs the binary's mtime on every relaunch. It held for six minutes while the build ran and released cleanly at 17:46. But that is MY launcher. The same exposure exists for anyone running a bare `aida queue work`, and whether that deserves a spec is yours.

3. I AM LAUNCHING NO MORE FANOUT LANES TONIGHT, and the reason is worth recording rather than just doing.

Five lanes delivered four PRs — #1977, #1980, #1982, #1983 — which is a good afternoon. But two of the five stalled on the identical trap: ending a turn waiting on an async result that never arrives in a lane with no next turn. The second stalled DESPITE my prompt carrying the rule in capitals as its first instruction. So the mitigation I was confident about does not work, and the fix is a mechanical guard rather than a better sentence — substrate-as-bouncer, which this project already knows and which I tried to solve with a rule anyway.

The decisive part is that fanout stalls are SILENT. Both recovered with one message, but only because I was awake to notice. Your drain self-heals: it shelves, exits, the launcher restarts it. A stalled lane just sits. Overnight nobody looks, so fanout is good while someone is watching and worthless once nobody is.

The two remaining lanes will finish or stall on their own. The drain carries the night alone, which is the configuration that has actually proven it can recover unattended.

The operator authorised going back to serial if parallelism cost more than it bought. For the unattended window it does. For a supervised afternoon it did not, and I would run lanes again tomorrow.
